extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent applicants/patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Alice/Mayo two-part patent-eligibility test (35 U.S.C. §101), including considerations for improvements to technology, use of a particular machine, particular transformations, and whether additional elements are well‑understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in existing technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of whether the claimed invention provides an improvement in existing technology; an improvement in technology (e.g., improving computers or a technical process) supports eligibility, whereas an improvement in an abstract idea itself does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration applies across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). Examples of sufficient improvements include McRO (specific rules improving animation automation) and Rapid Litigation Management (preserving hepatocytes). An improvement that merely enhances an abstract idea or business process without improving technology is insufficient (e.g., Trading Technologies where UI simply provided more information). To be persuasive, claims should show how they improve the technological process rather than claiming only the idea or outcome. See list of court-recognized examples (particular computerized methods, new telephone/server combinations, improved compression methods, GUIs that improve accuracy, improved biological preservation methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to recite how a computer aids the method
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that the involvement of a computer assists in improving technology, the claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding generic computer components or generic instructions to perform a method on a computer is not sufficient. The claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on generic machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for additional guidance about mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration (M-or-T as a clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the judicial exception is applied with or by use of a particular machine is an important clue for eligibility, but it is not a stand-alone test; all claims must still be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative tool but satisfying (or failing) it alone does not determine eligibility. If a claim passes Alice/Mayo it is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; if it fails Alice/Mayo it is ineligible even if it passes M-or-T. Examiners should also consider related analyses (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use) and consult MPEP §2106.03 for definition of 'machine'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the degree to which the machine/apparatus in the claim can be specifically identified (i.e., whether the elements are particular rather than generic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim reciting a particular type of machine with structural details (e.g., specific antenna shape/length/angles or Fourdrinier machine components arranged in a particular way) supports finding a particular machine. By contrast, a general-purpose computer that applies an exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine. Merely reciting concrete/tangible components or a 'specially programmed' generic computer does not automatically supply significantly more than the exception (see Ultramercial, TLI, Eon, Alappat, Bilski, Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the machine is integrally used to achieve performance of the claimed method (i.e., the machine 'plays a significant part' in permitting the claimed method to be performed), as opposed to being merely an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral use of a machine may integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more; a machine that merely acts as an obvious mechanism to achieve a solution (or that cannot itself perform the claimed steps) will not. See CyberSource (Internet cannot perform fraud-detection steps) and Versata (machine must play significant part rather than merely permitting faster achievement). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for further discussion of invoking computers/machinery merely as tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus merely contributing nominally (e.g., data-gathering or field-of-use limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (for instance, merely providing a source of data or a field-of-use limitation) typically does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Data-gathering steps and mere field-of-use limitations are frequently insufficient (see Bilski, CyberSource). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a clue to patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a particular, specifically-identified physical object or substance into a different state or thing (e.g., chemical transformations, curing/molding raw materials) is more likely to supply significantly more than an exception. Transformation is not a stand-alone test—claims still must pass Alice/Mayo. Mental processes or mere manipulation of abstract data/math constructs are not considered eligible transformations. See Bilski, Gottschalk v. Benson, Tilghman v. Proctor, Diamond v. Diehr for examples and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how particular or definite the recited transformation is (more particular transformations are more likely to provide significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing, smelting) show that definite chemical/physical acts that change articles in specific ways confine the monopoly within definite bounds and favor eligibility. A more particular transformation is likelier to be persuasive than a vague, high-level one (Gottschalk v. Benson discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the article being transformed is specifically identified or is generic/recited broadly (transformations limited to particular articles are more persuasive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation applied to a generically recited article or to 'any and all articles' is less likely to provide significantly more than the judicial exception. Specific identification of the article or limiting the claim to particular articles tends to favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and extent of the transformation (type/extent of change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the transformation changes the article's state or thing in a meaningful way (a new/different function or use) rather than merely changing location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations that produce a different function or use (e.g., raw uncured material to precision-molded product) are more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation or insignificant change in state is less persuasive. See Diamond v. Diehr example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the article transformed (physical vs intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the transformation is applied to a physical/tangible object or to an intangible concept (physical transformations are more likely to be significant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of a physical/tangible object or substance is more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application than transformation of an intangible concept (such as contractual obligations or mental judgments). Purely mental processes are not considered eligible transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the recited transformation meaningfully limits the claimed method or whether it is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to claim execution (e.g., merely administering a drug that the Supreme Court viewed as a field-of-use limitation in Mayo) will not provide significantly more than the judicial exception. See Mayo and discussion in MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, determine whether additional elements (beyond the judicial exception) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the art; such elements do not support a finding of 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are specific/unconventional and confine the claim to a particular useful application, this favors eligibility (example: DDR Holdings where additional elements dynamically produced a hybrid webpage). If additional elements are merely well-understood, routine, conventional activities recited at a high level of generality, they do not amount to an inventive concept (example: Mayo where measuring metabolites by known techniques was routine). This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, and insignificant extra-solution activity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether additional elements are well-understood/routine (analysis points)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether additional elements amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, examiners should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity and may use other Step 2B considerations to assist this determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points include: (1) an element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine for eligibility purposes (novelty/obviousness are separate questions); (2) overlap with improvement, mere-instructions, and insignificant extra-solution considerations should be used to inform the analysis. Enfish example: features known in prior art can still be unconventional in their application and thus support eligibility.
